hook.text: Behind an API, the data has to live somewhere, and usually that's a database. Its reads have to be fast, and its writes have to be right, even when another write lands at the same moment.

hook-run.text: Every number here comes from a run in Postgres, the open-source relational database, on a million users, a million orders, and a few small tables.

plan.text: Sixteen questions, plus one from system design. Eleven are worked through, and five go quickly at the end.

nosql.text: Question one. SQL versus NoSQL, when do you pick each? And from system design: SQL or NoSQL at scale, how do you choose?
nosql.spoken: Question one. Sequel versus no-sequel, when do you pick each? And from system design: sequel or no-sequel at scale, how do you choose?

nosql-sql.text: Pick relational when the data is structured and its relationships matter: joins, transactions across several rows, strong consistency. It's the safe default for most applications.

nosql-no.text: Pick NoSQL when writes must scale out across machines, when the schema keeps changing, which suits a document store, or when one access pattern, known in advance, runs at huge volume, which suits key-value or wide-column. The price: weaker consistency and limited joins.
nosql-no.spoken: Pick no-sequel when writes must scale out across machines, when the schema keeps changing, which suits a document store, or when one access pattern, known in advance, runs at huge volume, which suits key-value or wide-column. The price: weaker consistency and limited joins.

nosql-both.text: At scale, many systems use both: SQL for the core transactions, NoSQL for high-volume logs, sessions or feeds.
nosql-both.spoken: At scale, many systems use both: sequel for the core transactions, no-sequel for high-volume logs, sessions or feeds.

nosql-next.text: So ask which queries you'll need next year. Relational answers a new one with a join; a store built around one access pattern may need the data copied again, arranged for the new one.

index.text: Question two. What is a database index, and how does it speed up queries?

index-scan.text: Find one email among a million users without an index, and Postgres reads all seven thousand three hundred sixty pages of the table to keep one row.

index-tree.text: An index is a separate structure mapping values to their rows, usually a B-tree, balanced and sorted. This one is three levels deep, so the lookup reads three index pages and one table page: four pages, not seven thousand.

index-log.text: That's log n against n, and because the tree is sorted, it answers ranges too.

index-hash.text: The kind matters. A hash index goes straight to one email, but ask it for a range, and Postgres reads the whole table again.

hurt.text: Question three. When does an index help, and when does it hurt? It helps selective reads: equality, ranges, joins, and sorts on the column.

hurt-half.text: It does nothing when most rows match. Half the users are active, and even with an index on that column, Postgres scans the table: one pass beats half a million jumps.

hurt-writes.text: And every index costs writes. Ten thousand inserts wrote ten thousand log records with no index, and forty thousand with three, because each insert updates every index too.

hurt-space.text: They take space as well: together, the users table's three indexes are bigger than the table itself.

hurt-rule.text: So index the columns you filter and join on, not every column.

composite.text: Question four. What is a composite index, and why does column order matter? It sorts by its first column, then by the second within each value of the first, like a phone book: last name, then first name.

composite-prefix.text: So it serves a left prefix: every Lovelace, or Ada Lovelace, but not every Ada.

composite-run.text: An index on customer, then order time, finds customer forty-two's ten latest orders in thirteen pages, already newest first, with no sort.

composite-day.text: Ask it for one day across all customers, and Postgres reads the table instead.

composite-swap.text: Swap the two columns, and the same ten orders cost over eighteen hundred pages.

composite-rule.text: So order the columns by your queries: equality first, then the range or the sort.

composite-skip.text: Postgres eighteen added a skip scan, which uses an index without its first column when that column has few values. On status, then order time, one day took five index searches and never touched the table.

plan-q.text: Question five. How do you read a query plan? Explain analyze runs the query and prints its plan as a tree: the indented step runs first and feeds the one above it.

plan-look.text: Read three things: the kind of scan, the estimated rows against the actual rows, and the rows a filter threw away.

plan-bad.text: This count of one day's orders scans the table, though order time has an index. It expected five thousand rows, found two thousand seven hundred thirty-two, and threw away nearly a million.

plan-why.text: The cause is the filter. It turns each timestamp into a date, and an index on a column can't search a function of it.

plan-fix.text: Write it as a range on the column itself, and the plan becomes an index-only scan, with an estimate that's exactly right.

plan-sarg.text: That's a sargable filter: one the index can search.

fanout.text: Question six. Why can a join inflate a sum, and how do you fix it? Joining to a one-to-many table repeats each row once per match.

fanout-run.text: Join the page's twenty-four orders to their line items, to count those too, and each order repeats once per item: forty-eight rows, and the revenue more than doubles. Sara's three hundred four dollars becomes nine hundred twelve, since both her orders have three items.

fanout-fix.text: Fix it by aggregating the many side to the right grain first: count the items per order, then join. One row per order, and the revenue is right again.

fanout-check.text: Check the row count before and after every join.

txn.text: Question seven. What is a transaction, and how do you use one? It groups statements so they succeed or fail as one: begin, run them, then commit, or roll back.

txn-run.text: Here's a transfer of thirty. The debit takes account one to seventy. Then recording the transfer fails: account ninety-nine doesn't exist, and the foreign key refuses it.

txn-abort.text: Postgres now refuses every statement until the transaction ends. Roll back, and account one is at a hundred again. The application's job is to catch the error, roll back, and retry or report it, never carry on.

levels.text: Question eight. What are the SQL isolation levels? The standard names four: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, and serializable. Each is defined by the anomalies it rules out, not by how it's built, and defaults differ: Postgres uses read committed.
levels.spoken: Question eight. What are the sequel isolation levels? The standard names four: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, and serializable. Each is defined by the anomalies it rules out, not by how it's built, and defaults differ: Postgres uses read committed.

anomalies.text: Question nine. What anomalies do isolation levels prevent? Three classic ones.

anomalies-dirty.text: A dirty read sees another transaction's change before it commits. Here another transaction set the balance to fifty, uncommitted. Postgres never shows it: at all four levels, even read uncommitted, the read says a hundred.

anomalies-nonrep.text: A non-repeatable read: read a row twice, another transaction commits a change in between, and the second read differs. Read committed allows it; repeatable read prevents it.

anomalies-phantom.text: A phantom: rerun a query, and new rows match, because another transaction inserted them. The standard stops phantoms only at serializable; Postgres's repeatable read already does.

anomalies-serial.text: Serializable promises an outcome some one-at-a-time order could give.

lock.text: Question ten. What is an optimistic versus pessimistic locking strategy? Pessimistic locks first: select for update locks the row until commit, and any other transaction that wants to change or lock it waits.

lock-pess-run.text: Here another transaction holds account one. Asked not to wait, Postgres refuses: it could not obtain the lock. Account two is free.

lock-opt.text: Optimistic takes no lock. Read a version number with the row, and write only if it hasn't changed.

lock-opt-run.text: Two clients read version three. One writes, and the version becomes four. The other's write, still expecting three, changes nothing. It rereads, and retries.

lock-choose.text: Optimistic wins when conflicts are rare, since one costs only a retry. Pessimistic wins when they're frequent, and retries would pile up.

deadlock.text: Question eleven. What is a deadlock, and how do you avoid it? A cycle of transactions, each holding a lock another one needs.

deadlock-cycle.text: Two transfers start together. One locks account one, then wants account two. The other locks account two, then wants account one. Neither can go on.

deadlock-detect.text: Postgres waits one second, its deadlock timeout, then looks for a cycle. It finds this one and aborts a transaction, the victim, with a deadlock error. The other finishes, and the application retries the victim.

deadlock-order.text: To avoid it, take locks in one global order, say the lowest account ID first: the second transfer then simply waits, and no cycle forms. Keep transactions short, and use the lowest isolation level that's correct.

rapid-in.text: Five more, a sentence or two each.

r-acid.text: ACID: atomicity, all or nothing; consistency, every constraint holds; isolation, concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other; durability, a commit survives a crash.
r-acid.spoken: Acid: atomicity, all or nothing; consistency, every constraint holds; isolation, concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other; durability, a commit survives a crash.

r-norm.text: Normalization stores each fact once, so no update leaves copies disagreeing, which suits write-heavy systems. Denormalization repeats data to skip joins, buying read speed with storage and harder updates. Normalize first; denormalize where profiling blames a join.

r-joins.text: Joins differ in which unmatched rows survive. Inner keeps only matches: twenty-four rows. Left keeps every customer, with nulls where there's no order: thirty, for the six who never ordered. Right mirrors it, and full keeps both sides.

r-keys.text: A primary key identifies each row: unique, never null, and indexed automatically. A foreign key points at another table's primary key, so no order can name a missing customer. Postgres doesn't index the foreign key's column for you.

r-cover.text: A covering index holds every column a query needs, so Postgres answers from the index alone, with zero trips to the table, at the price of a wider index.

next.text: Isolation, locks and deadlocks are the database's side of one problem: many requests arriving at once. Next: concurrency.

anomalies-abort.text: In exchange, Postgres may abort a transaction with a serialization failure, to be retried.

nosql-scale.text: Relational scales further than people think, with replicas and sharding, so decide on the access pattern and the consistency you need, not on size alone.

plan-gap.text: Postgres picks its plan from that estimate, so a big gap means a bad choice, like a nested loop over far more rows than it guessed.

plan-fixes.text: The other usual fixes: an index on the expression itself, or fresh statistics when the estimates are stale.

fanout-grow.text: The error grows with the items per order, so a test on single-item orders can hide it.

anomalies-skew.text: That stops write skew, which repeatable read allows: two transactions each check a rule, then each change a different row, and together they break it.

lock-cost.text: Pessimistic makes others wait, which costs throughput and risks deadlocks. And across two requests, with no transaction held open, only optimistic works: send the version back with the write.

r-keys-fix.text: Index it yourself, or finding a customer's orders, or deleting a customer, scans the whole orders table.
